correctness.rationale: The code fixes the 16-vertex Cayley graph, checks the strongly regular parameters, and enumerates all 65536 masks using both the closed-neighborhood exclusion predicate and the direct dominating-complement predicate. Both yield 53730 nonempty faces. The explicit certificate has 26799 distinct matched Hasse covers with exactly one critical vertex and 131 critical 9-faces. A full directed Hasse graph with 401088 edges is topologically sorted over all 53730 face vertices, so acyclicity is proved by exhaustive finite computation, not an experiment. Forman's theorem gives a CW model with one 0-cell and 131 9-cells; its attaching maps are necessarily constant. Euler check gives -131; every artifact is included and executable without external dependencies.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The proposed statement is equivalent to an integral homotopy classification of the closed-neighborhood-avoidance hypergraph complex. Ordinary independence forbids edges, whereas dominance forbids entire six-vertex closed neighborhoods; a classification of Ind(C) does not imply the rank 131 result. Combinatorial Alexander duality connects homology of D(C) with cohomology of N(complement C), but the checked Clebsch neighborhood theorem concerns N(C); the graphs are not isomorphic since their degrees differ (five versus ten).

value.rationale: The five-regular Clebsch graph is the canonical 16-vertex folded cube with strongly regular parameters (16,5,0,2), whose dominance complex is not classified by the forest, chordal, cycle or path-product theorems. This complete integral homotopy result gives a motivated natural benchmark, determines the previously unreported rank and dimension of all homology, and is stronger than an Euler-characteristic or one-field table. The face complex reaches dimension eleven but has homotopy concentrated in nine, revealing a meaningful nontrivial collapse in a symmetric graph beyond standard classes. The finite exact invariant and its reproducible proof are useful even without an infinite-family theorem.
